components.note: 亻 (person) — represents a human figure.

叚 depicts borrowing or handing something over — a person who is not genuine, or something borrowed rather than real, gave 假 its meaning 'false, fake' (and, for a break from routine, 'vacation, leave.')
衣 (clothing) — 装 relates to clothes, dress, and attire
壮 (zhuàng) gives the sound — 装 is pronounced zhuāng, a close match

example.hanzi: 他假装没听到我说的话。
example.pinyin: Tā jiǎzhuāng méi tīngdào wǒ shuō de huà.
example.english: He pretended not to hear what I said.
example.fact: 假 on its own already means “fake, false” (as in 假货, “counterfeit goods”), and 装 can independently mean “to dress up, put on an act” (装傻, “play dumb”) — 假装 stacks two words that both point toward artifice, a common way Mandarin builds a two-character verb from near-synonyms.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.
走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.

example.hanzi: 这首歌让我想起了童年。
example.pinyin: Zhè shǒu gē ràng wǒ xiǎngqǐ le tóngnián.
example.english: This song reminds me of my childhood.
example.fact: 想起 is a verb-plus-complement pair: 想 (“to think”) combines with 起, literally “to rise,” used here as a directional complement — a memory “rising up” into awareness. The same 起 carries a related sense in 起来's “coming into being” usage.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 侦 describes a person who investigates or spies.
贞 (zhēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 侦.
扌 (hand) — 探 describes reaching out with the hand to search for something.

example.hanzi: 那位侦探很快就找到了线索。
example.pinyin: Nà wèi zhēntàn hěn kuài jiù zhǎodào le xiànsuǒ.
example.english: That detective quickly found a clue.
example.fact: 侦探 as a compound job title pairs two overlapping “to investigate” verbs — 侦 (“to scout, spy on”) and 探 (“to probe, explore”) — reinforcing near-synonyms into one word, a common Mandarin word-building strategy.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 验 originally related to examining or testing horses, later extended to 'to test, examine, verify'
佥 (qiān) gives a loose sound connection to 验's reading yàn
宀 (roof) — 室 refers to an enclosed room under a roof
至 (zhì) gives the sound — an exact match with 室's reading shì

example.hanzi: 科学家们在实验室里做实验。
example.pinyin: Kēxuéjiā men zài shíyànshì lǐ zuò shíyàn.
example.english: The scientists are doing experiments in the laboratory.
example.fact: 实验室 is just 实验 (“experiment,” from 实 “real, actual” + 验 “to test, verify”) plus the suffix 室 (“room”) — the same room-naming suffix behind 教室 (“classroom”) and 办公室 (“office”), a reliable pattern for naming a room by what happens inside it.

components.note: 页 (head) is the semantic root here, though the exact link to 顺's meaning 'to follow' isn't fully clear today.
川 (chuān) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading shùn has diverged.

example.hanzi: 你去超市的话,顺便帮我买一瓶牛奶吧。
example.pinyin: Nǐ qù chāoshì dehuà, shùnbiàn bāng wǒ mǎi yì píng niúnǎi ba.
example.english: If you're going to the supermarket, could you pick up a bottle of milk for me while you're at it?
example.fact: 顺便 almost always attaches to a request or suggestion (顺便 + verb), politely framing a favor as no extra trouble — it signals the action is being done “along the way,” piggybacking on something already planned, much like English “while you're at it.”

components.note: 戈 (a spear or weapon) — 或 pictures defending a territory.
口 (here representing a walled area or territory) — defending one's territory with a weapon gave 或 its early sense of 'a certain place,' which later shifted to mean 'or,' offering an alternative.
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 你可以喝茶或是喝咖啡。
example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ hē chá huòshì hē kāfēi.
example.english: You can drink tea or coffee.
example.fact: 或 alone can already mean “or” by itself; the following 是 isn't the verb “to be” here but a light, semantically bleached suffix that pads a one-syllable connector into a smoother two-syllable one — a similar non-literal role 是 plays in conjunctions like 但是 (“but”) and 要是 (“if”).

meanings: (often used in the negative) to care about

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.hanzi: 别人怎么想,他一点也不在乎。
example.pinyin: Biérén zěnme xiǎng, tā yìdiǎn yě bú zàihu.
example.english: He doesn't care at all what other people think.
example.fact: Although older dictionary senses for 在乎 include formal phrases like “to rest with” or “to be due to,” in everyday Mandarin it overwhelmingly means “to care” — and it shows up far more often in its negative form 不在乎 (“doesn't care”) than as a bare positive claim, much as English “mind” reads more naturally in “I don't mind” than in a positive statement.

components.note: 耳 (ear) — chatting involves listening as well as speaking.
卯 (mǎo) gives a sound distantly related to liáo, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 这部电影太无聊了,我们中途就走了。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng tài wúliáo le, wǒmen zhōngtú jiù zǒu le.
example.english: This movie was so boring that we left partway through.
example.fact: 无聊 can describe either the boring situation or the bored person feeling it, without changing form — Mandarin adjectives like this rely entirely on context to sort out the active/passive reading that English marks with “-ing” versus “-ed” (boring vs. bored).

components.note: 犬 (dog) — an old, now-opaque link behind 状's meaning 'form, shape, condition'
丬 (qiáng) gives a loose sound connection to 状's reading zhuàng

example.hanzi: 医生说她的身体状况已经稳定了。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng shuō tā de shēntǐ zhuàngkuàng yǐjīng wěndìng le.
example.english: The doctor said her physical condition has stabilized.
example.fact: 状况 and its near-synonym 情况 both translate as “situation,” but 状况 leans toward a measurable, observable state — health, equipment, finances — while 情况 more often frames a broader, unfolding circumstance, a distinction dictionaries frequently gloss identically.

components.note: 目 depicts an eye turned on its side, with the outline and pupil visible — later straightened into today's rectangular shape.

example.hanzi: 他学中文的目的是想去中国工作。
example.pinyin: Tā xué Zhōngwén de mùdì shì xiǎng qù Zhōngguó gōngzuò.
example.english: His purpose in learning Chinese is to go work in China.
example.fact: 目的 combines 目 (“eye”) with 的, which in Classical Chinese specifically meant “a target for archery” — literally “what the eye is aimed at,” a vivid compositional image behind today's abstract word for “purpose, goal.”

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恶 relates to an evil or malicious state of heart/mind
亚 (yà) gives a sound distantly related to 恶's reading è, having drifted apart over time
鬼 (ghost) — 魔 names a demon or evil spirit.
麻 (má) gives a sound distantly related to mó, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 故事里的恶魔想要毁灭整个世界。
example.pinyin: Gùshi lǐ de èmó xiǎng yào huǐmiè zhěng gè shìjiè.
example.english: The demon in the story wants to destroy the entire world.
example.fact: 魔 was coined specifically to carry a foreign sound: early Buddhist translators first wrote Sanskrit “māra” (a demon who tempted the Buddha) as 磨 (“to grind”), and Emperor Wu of Liang is credited with swapping its 石 radical for 鬼 (“ghost”) to produce 魔 — one of a small set of Chinese characters invented mainly to carry a loanword's sound, later broadening into today's everyday word for “demon, magic.”

components.note: 石 (stone) — 确 originally meant firm and solid like stone, extending to 'true, accurate, indeed.'
角 (jiǎo) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from què.
亻 (person) — 保 relates to a person looking after or protecting someone, originally a caretaker holding a child.
呆 (dāi) gives a hint of the sound — 保 is pronounced bǎo, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 请检查门窗,确保一切安全。
example.pinyin: Qǐng jiǎnchá ménchuāng, quèbǎo yíqiè ānquán.
example.english: Please check the doors and windows to make sure everything is safe.
example.fact: 确保 sits at the formal end of Mandarin's “make sure” vocabulary — official announcements, safety instructions, and contracts reach for it, where casual speech more often just uses 保证 (“promise, guarantee”) or a plain 一定 (“definitely”); using 确保 in everyday conversation can sound a little stiff.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.
⺼ (flesh) shows 脏 (zàng) relates to the body, as in internal organs.
庄 (zhuāng) gives a sound close to zàng, sharing a similar consonant sound though the vowel and ending differ.

example.hanzi: 医生用听诊器检查了他的心脏。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng yòng tīngzhěnqì jiǎnchá le tā de xīnzàng.
example.english: The doctor used a stethoscope to examine his heart.
example.fact: 心脏 is the precise anatomical term for the physical heart organ, built from 心 (“heart”) plus 脏 (zàng, “internal organ”) — for the emotional or figurative “heart” (feelings, courage, the heart of a matter), Mandarin instead reaches for the bare 心 alone, a split English's single word “heart” doesn't make.

components.note: 亻 (a person), shown twice — one person next to another, similar in shape, the source of 似's meaning 'to resemble, similar, like.'

example.hanzi: 他跑得飞快,像箭似的。
example.pinyin: Tā pǎo de fēikuài, xiàng jiàn shìde.
example.english: He ran incredibly fast, like an arrow.
example.fact: 似 is pronounced sì almost everywhere else in Mandarin (相似, “similar”), but Mainland dictionaries specifically mark this one grammatical suffix as shìde — Taiwan usage instead keeps the more predictable sìde, making 似的 one of the few words where the Mainland-standard reading is the less intuitive one to memorize.

components.note: 無-shaped top pictures a dancer holding decorated sleeves or fans.
舛 below pictures a pair of feet, together giving 舞 its meaning 'to dance.'
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.hanzi: 学校下周六举办一场舞会。
example.pinyin: Xuéxiào xià zhōu liù jǔbàn yì chǎng wǔhuì.
example.english: The school is holding a dance next Saturday.
example.fact: 舞会 pairs 舞 (“dance”) with 会 in its “gathering, meeting” sense — the same sense behind 社会 (“society,” also in this batch) — rather than 会's more familiar “to know how to” sense, a reminder that the character carries two genuinely separate meanings depending on context.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.
方 (a flag/banner) — a shared banner under which a group gathers.
矢 (arrow) — warriors bound by oath under one flag gave 族 its meaning 'clan, ethnic group, tribe.'

example.hanzi: 这个家族已经在这座城市生活了几百年。
example.pinyin: Zhège jiāzú yǐjīng zài zhè zuò chéngshì shēnghuó le jǐ bǎi nián.
example.english: This family has lived in this city for hundreds of years.
example.fact: 家族 refers to an extended clan or lineage spanning generations, distinct from 家庭 (“family” in the narrower sense of one household — parents and children) — conflating the two is a common learner slip, since English “family” covers both senses with a single word.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 慢 describes an unhurried state of mind or pace.
曼 (màn) gives the sound — an exact match with 慢.
忄 (heart) — 慢 describes an unhurried state of mind or pace.
曼 (màn) gives the sound — an exact match with 慢.

example.hanzi: 请慢慢说,我听不太懂。
example.pinyin: Qǐng mànmàn shuō, wǒ tīng bú tài dǒng.
example.english: Please speak slowly, I don't quite understand.
example.fact: Reduplicating a one-syllable adjective like 慢 into 慢慢 is one of Mandarin's most productive ways to turn a description into a gentle adverb of manner — in fast, casual speech the second syllable often gets a light neutral-toned “mān” rather than the full fourth tone, even though dictionaries still print it as màn.

components.note: 戈 (a dagger-axe, a weapon) — 战 relates to fighting and war.
占 (zhàn) gives the sound — 战 is also pronounced zhàn, an exact match.
斗 depicts a hand-held dipper or ladle used for measuring grain and liquids — giving 斗 its meaning 'a unit of dry measure,' and by extension, the Big Dipper constellation.

example.hanzi: 士兵们在战斗中表现得非常勇敢。
example.pinyin: Shìbīng men zài zhàndòu zhōng biǎoxiàn de fēicháng yǒnggǎn.
example.english: The soldiers showed great courage in the battle.
example.fact: 战斗 sits at the serious, organized-combat end of Mandarin's “fight” vocabulary — a schoolyard scuffle or a shouting match instead reaches for 打架 or 吵架, reserving 战斗 for war, military combat, or a figuratively hard-fought struggle.

components.note: 亻 (a person) — the one repeating the routine.
日 (day, sun) — going somewhere every day, a repeated routine giving 复 its meaning 'to repeat, return; again.'

example.hanzi: 这道数学题太复杂了,我做不出来。
example.pinyin: Zhè dào shùxué tí tài fùzá le, wǒ zuò bu chūlái.
example.english: This math problem is too complicated, I can't solve it.
example.fact: 复 alone already carries a sense of “repeating, compounding” (as in 复习, “to review”), so 复杂 literally suggests something with many layers stacked on top of each other — its clean opposite, 简单 (“simple”), is one of the first antonym pairs Mandarin learners memorize.

components.note: 礻 (an altar, related to ritual) — 社 relates to worship and community gatherings.
土 (earth) — ancient communities worshipped a local earth spirit together, giving 社 its meaning 'society' or 'community.'
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.hanzi: 教育对社会的发展非常重要。
example.pinyin: Jiàoyù duì shèhuì de fāzhǎn fēicháng zhòngyào.
example.english: Education is very important for the development of society.
example.fact: 社 originally named the local earth-god shrine that a village community gathered around to worship — 社会's modern sense of “society” grew directly out of that older image of a community bound together by a shared gathering place.

components.note: 攵 (an action) — ties to 故's sense of a cause or reason behind an action
古 (gǔ) gives a sound close to 故's reading gù
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.hanzi: 我不是故意的,真的很抱歉。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bú shì gùyì de, zhēn de hěn bàoqiàn.
example.english: I didn't do it on purpose, I'm really sorry.
example.fact: “不是故意的” (“I didn't mean to”) is one of the most common apologies in spoken Mandarin, with 故意 as its key word — its natural comeback, 不小心 (“carelessly, accidentally”), is worth learning alongside it as the paired excuse.

components.note: 阝 (mound, place) shows 邻 relates to a nearby location.
令 (lìng) gives a sound close to lín, sharing the initial consonant.
户 (door) — 居 relates to where one lives, behind a door
古 (gǔ) gives a sound related to 居's reading jū, from an older, closer pronunciation link

example.hanzi: 我们的邻居非常友好,经常互相帮忙。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de línjū fēicháng yǒuhǎo, jīngcháng hùxiāng bāngmáng.
example.english: Our neighbors are very friendly, and we often help each other out.
example.fact: 邻居 combines 邻 (“adjacent, nearby”) with 居 (“to reside, dwell”) — literally “one who dwells nearby.” English “neighbor” is built the same way, from Old English “nēah” (near) plus “gebūr” (dweller) — two unrelated languages independently landing on the identical logic.

components.note: 亼 — traditionally linked to an image of gathering or covering; its original pictorial sense has become obscure, but the character came to mean 'now, the present.'
干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'

example.hanzi: 今年夏天特别热。
example.pinyin: Jīnnián xiàtiān tèbié rè.
example.english: This summer has been especially hot.
example.fact: 今年, 今天 (“today”), and 今晚 (“tonight”) all share the prefix 今 (“the present, now”) — once a learner spots this one recurring syllable, the whole family of “this ___” time words becomes predictable rather than needing separate memorization.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.
田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.hanzi: 我心里一直想着这件事。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xīnli yìzhí xiǎngzhe zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: I've been thinking about this the whole time, deep down.
example.fact: 心里 literally means “inside the heart” (心 “heart” + 里 “inside”) and is Mandarin's default way to talk about private, unspoken thoughts — 心里想 (“to think to oneself”) describes something felt internally, in contrast to 说 (“to say”), which brings a thought out into the open.

components.note: 尸 (here representing a covering or stall, not a corpse) — 展 pictures a place where goods are displayed.
衣 (clothing) — clothing laid out for display gave 展 its meaning 'to unfold' or 'to exhibit.'
A pictograph of an altar or offering table used in ancestor worship — presenting offerings extended to 示's meaning 'to show, display, indicate.'

example.hanzi: 这家博物馆展示了很多古代文物。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā bówùguǎn zhǎnshì le hěn duō gǔdài wénwù.
example.english: This museum displays many ancient artifacts.
example.fact: 展示 leans formal — exhibitions, presentations, formal demonstrations — while casual speech more often just says 给...看 (“show to...”); the newer slangy 秀 (a phonetic loanword from English “show,” as in 脱口秀, “talk show”) covers similar ground with a much more casual flavor.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
禾 (grain, a growing rice or wheat plant) — 利 pictures a harvest.
刂 (knife) — cutting grain at harvest time was a clear benefit or gain, giving 利 its meaning 'profit' or 'advantage.'

example.hanzi: 他们打算下个月去意大利旅游。
example.pinyin: Tāmen dǎsuàn xià gè yuè qù Yìdàlì lǚyóu.
example.english: They're planning to travel to Italy next month.
example.fact: 意大利 is a phonetic transliteration of “Italia” — the three characters were picked mainly to approximate the sound (Yì-dà-lì), not for their literal meanings, the same strategy behind most Mandarin names for countries outside the historical Sinosphere, like 加拿大 (Jiānádà) for “Canada.”

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.
讠 (speech) — represents words being spoken.
斥 (to reprimand, blame) — words of accusation or complaint gave 诉 its meaning 'to sue, to tell, to complain.'

example.hanzi: 他决定起诉那家公司。
example.pinyin: Tā juédìng qǐsù nà jiā gōngsī.
example.english: He decided to sue that company.
example.fact: 起诉 is a formal legal term reserved for actually filing a lawsuit or bringing criminal charges — an everyday grievance instead reaches for much softer words like 抱怨 (“to complain”) or 投诉 (“to file a complaint,” e.g. to customer service), so hearing 起诉 signals the matter has escalated to court.

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 他是个乐于助人的好人。
example.pinyin: Tā shì gè lèyú zhùrén de hǎorén.
example.english: He's a good person who loves helping others.
example.fact: 好人 is about as literal a compound as Mandarin offers — 好 (“good”) plus 人 (“person”) — but its very plainness is why it needs careful handling: in modern slang, calling someone a 好人 can faintly imply “nice, but a pushover” (as in 好人卡, the “good-person card” of being turned down romantically), so tone and context matter more than the dictionary gloss suggests.

components.note: 囗 (a boundary/enclosure) surrounding 玉 (jade, treasure) — a country pictured as protected, valuable territory.
十 — traditionally read as a great man standing tall.
一 (the two horizontal strokes) — heaven above and earth below, which the king bridges, giving 王 its meaning 'king, monarch.'

example.hanzi: 这个国家的国王非常受人民爱戴。
example.pinyin: Zhège guójiā de guówáng fēicháng shòu rénmín àidài.
example.english: This country's king is deeply loved by his people.
example.fact: 王 by itself already meant “king, monarch” (it's also the common surname Wáng, originally a title before it became a family name) — 国王 clarifies the specifically national, ruling sense by prefixing 国 (“country, state”), setting it apart from other extended uses of 王 like 龙王, the mythological “Dragon King.”

components.note: 长 (simplified from 長) depicts an elderly figure with long flowing hair and a cane — length and seniority are linked in the original picture.
A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'

example.hanzi: 我在北京长大,但现在住在上海。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài Běijīng zhǎngdà, dàn xiànzài zhù zài Shànghǎi.
example.english: I grew up in Beijing, but now I live in Shanghai.
example.fact: 长 is a genuine two-way character: read cháng it means “long” (长城, “the Great Wall”), and read zhǎng it means “to grow, to be senior” (长大, 家长 “parent”) — one character splitting into two unrelated pronunciations and meaning-families, with no visual cue to tell them apart.

components.note: Depicts a person standing with legs crossed — the crossing shape gave 交 its meaning 'to intersect, exchange, hand over.'
纟 (thread/silk) — 给 originally related to supplying thread or material, later broadening to mean 'to give.'
合 (hé) gives a hint of the sound — 给 is pronounced gěi, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 我把钱交给了银行职员。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ qián jiāo gěi le yínháng zhíyuán.
example.english: I handed the money over to the bank clerk.
example.fact: 交给 commonly appears inside a 把-construction (把 + object + 交给 + recipient), fronting the thing being handed over before the verb — a pattern worth noticing for verbs describing a literal physical transfer, where 把 often reads more naturally than plain subject-verb-object order.

components.note: 阝 (mound, place) shows 陪 relates to being present alongside someone somewhere.
咅 gives a sound distantly related to péi, having drifted apart over time.
宀 (roof) — 审 relates to a formal setting, like a courtroom, where matters are examined
申 (shēn) gives a sound close to 审's reading shěn, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
才 (talent) — many talented people.
囗 (an enclosure) — gathered together in one place, giving 团 its meaning 'group, team; round, ball-shaped.'

example.hanzi: 陪审团经过三天讨论后做出了判决。
example.pinyin: Péishěntuán jīngguò sān tiān tǎolùn hòu zuòchū le pànjué.
example.english: After three days of deliberation, the jury reached a verdict.
example.fact: 陪审团 is a modern legal loan-translation coined for a Western institution — 陪审 (“to accompany in judging,” i.e., to serve as a juror) plus 团 (“group”). Mainland Chinese courts don't actually use jury trials, relying instead on a system of lay assessors, so the word shows up far more in translated foreign news and legal dramas than in domestic reporting.

components.note: 页 (head) — 项 originally referred to the back of the neck, near the head, later extended to mean 'item, sum'
工 (gōng) gives a loose sound connection to 项's reading xiàng
目 depicts an eye turned on its side, with the outline and pupil visible — later straightened into today's rectangular shape.

example.hanzi: 这个项目预计需要六个月才能完成。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiàngmù yùjì xūyào liù gè yuè cáinéng wánchéng.
example.english: This project is expected to take six months to complete.
example.fact: 项目 covers a surprising range of English words depending on context — “project” in business, “item” on a list or budget, “event” in sports (田径项目, “track and field event”) — one Mandarin compound doing the job of three fairly distinct English nouns.

components.note: 隹 (a bird) — one of a flock.
木 (a tree) — birds flocking together on a tree, the image of gathering that gave 集 its meaning 'to gather, collect; a collection.'
A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.hanzi: 请大家集中注意力,认真听讲。
example.pinyin: Qǐng dàjiā jízhōng zhùyìlì, rènzhēn tīngjiǎng.
example.english: Everyone please focus your attention and listen carefully.
example.fact: 集中 works as both a verb (“to concentrate, gather together”) and a stative description (“concentrated, centralized”) without changing form — covering both a physical gathering of things (人口集中, “the population is concentrated”) and a mental focusing of attention (集中注意力), two senses English usually keeps apart with different words.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'

example.hanzi: 说实话,我根本不喜欢这个计划。
example.pinyin: Shuō shíhuà, wǒ gēnběn bù xǐhuan zhège jìhuà.
example.english: To tell the truth, I don't like this plan at all.
example.fact: 实话 shows up almost exclusively inside the fixed opener “说实话” (“to speak honestly,” “to tell the truth”) — a discourse marker that, much like English “honestly” or “to be frank,” signals the speaker is about to say something candid, and possibly blunt.

components.note: 毛 (fur, hair) — 表 originally pictured a fur garment worn on the outside.
衣 (clothing) — an outer fur wrap gave 表 its meaning of 'outer' or 'surface,' and later, 'to express' (showing something on the surface).
忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 她听到这个消息后,脸上露出惊讶的表情。
example.pinyin: Tā tīngdào zhège xiāoxi hòu, liǎn shàng lùchū jīngyà de biǎoqíng.
example.english: After hearing the news, a look of surprise appeared on her face.
example.fact: 表情 combines 表 (“to show, express” — from an old image of a fur garment worn on the outside, hence “outer, surface”) with 情 (“feeling, emotion”) — literally “the outward showing of feeling,” a compositional logic that survives almost unchanged in the English loan-translation “facial expression.”

components.note: 目 (eye) — 冒 originally described something extending over or covering, related to a covering over the head.
冃 (mào) is an exact match for the sound of 冒.
阝 (hill) — 险 originally referred to steep, dangerous terrain
佥 (qiān) gives a sound distantly related to 险's reading xiǎn, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 他喜欢冒险,经常一个人去爬山。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan màoxiǎn, jīngcháng yí gè rén qù páshān.
example.english: He likes taking risks and often goes mountain climbing alone.
example.fact: 冒险 works as both a verb (“to take a risk”) and a noun (“an adventure”), letting one word cover ground English splits between “to risk” and “adventure” — 冒险家 (“adventurer”) and 冒险精神 (“adventurous spirit”) both build directly on the same root.

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
夂 (a foot, to go) — 处 relates to arriving somewhere.
卜 (a mark or flag) — planting a marker after arriving gave 处 its meaning of 'a place' or 'to settle, deal with.'

example.hanzi: 多喝水对身体有很多好处。
example.pinyin: Duō hē shuǐ duì shēntǐ yǒu hěn duō hǎochu.
example.english: Drinking more water has a lot of benefits for your health.
example.fact: The exact same two characters, with the second syllable kept in its full third tone as hǎochǔ, form a separate and much rarer word meaning “easy to get along with” — a tone-only homograph just like 告诉's rare legal-register reading elsewhere in this deck. The everyday, high-frequency word is this neutral-toned hǎochu, “benefit, advantage” — the sense used here.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吸 describes breathing in through the mouth.
及 (jí) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading xī has diverged.
皿 (a vessel) — a chalice or bowl
丿 — a single drop of blood inside the vessel
The 田-shaped top pictures a large, strange head.
儿-shaped legs below trace a crouching, spindly body, together giving 鬼 the shape of a ghostly figure.

example.hanzi: 这部电影讲述了一个吸血鬼的爱情故事。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng jiǎngshù le yí gè xīxuèguǐ de àiqíng gùshi.
example.english: This movie tells the love story of a vampire.
example.fact: 吸血鬼 is a literal, descriptive loan-translation rather than a phonetic borrowing of “vampire” — 吸血 (“to suck blood”) plus 鬼 (“ghost, spirit”). Unlike 意大利 (a purely sound-based transliteration also in this batch), this word was built entirely from existing Chinese roots to describe what a vampire does.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — historically linked to physical strength and overcoming an opponent
生 (shēng) gives a sound close to 胜's reading shèng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
禾 (grain, a growing rice or wheat plant) — 利 pictures a harvest.
刂 (knife) — cutting grain at harvest time was a clear benefit or gain, giving 利 its meaning 'profit' or 'advantage.'

example.hanzi: 我们的球队终于赢得了这场比赛的胜利。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de qiúduì zhōngyú yíngdé le zhè chǎng bǐsài de shènglì.
example.english: Our team finally achieved victory in this match.
example.fact: 胜利 doubles up two characters that each already point toward triumph on their own: 胜 (“to overcome, defeat,” as in 胜出 “to win out”) and 利 (“gain, advantage,” as in 利益 “benefit”) — pairing two near-synonyms into one intensified word, a common Mandarin strategy for building two-character verbs and nouns.

meanings: to go as far as to

components.note: 音 (music/sound) — a musical piece being performed
儿 (a person) — the performer finishing the piece
灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他竟然一个人爬上了那座山。
example.pinyin: Tā jìngrán yí gè rén pá shàng le nà zuò shān.
example.english: To my surprise, he climbed that mountain all by himself.
example.fact: 竟然 is an adverb of attitude rather than fact — it adds no new information to a sentence, only the speaker's surprise at it. Removing 竟然 leaves a sentence's literal meaning untouched while stripping out all the astonishment.

components.note: 並 (side by side, together) — represents everyone, all people.
日 (sun) — everyone standing together under the same sun gave 普 its meaning 'universal, general, widespread.'
辶 (to walk, movement) — 通 relates to passing through or getting somewhere.
甬 (yǒng) gives a hint of the sound — 通 is pronounced tōng, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 他只是一个普通的上班族,过着简单的生活。
example.pinyin: Tā zhǐshì yí gè pǔtōng de shàngbānzú, guòzhe jiǎndān de shēnghuó.
example.english: He's just an ordinary office worker, living a simple life.
example.fact: 普通 is the root behind 普通话 (“Putonghua,” literally “the common speech”), the official Mainland term for Standard Mandarin — the same “common, general” sense behind the everyday adjective also names the entire standardized national language.

components.note: 毛 (fur, hair) — 表 originally pictured a fur garment worn on the outside.
衣 (clothing) — an outer fur wrap gave 表 its meaning of 'outer' or 'surface,' and later, 'to express' (showing something on the surface).
A pictograph of an altar or offering table used in ancestor worship — presenting offerings extended to 示's meaning 'to show, display, indicate.'

example.hanzi: 他点了点头,表示同意。
example.pinyin: Tā diǎnle diǎn tóu, biǎoshì tóngyì.
example.english: He nodded his head, indicating his agreement.
example.fact: 表示 overlaps heavily with 表现 (“to show, display”) and 表达 (“to express,” usually feelings or ideas in words) — all three share the root 表 (“to show”) but attach different second characters to specialize: 示 for signaling, 现 for outward manifestation, 达 for conveying through language.

components.note: 爪 (a hand/claw) — pressing down.
卩 depicts a seal or stamp — a hand pressing a seal down gave 印 its meaning 'to print, seal, stamp.'
豕 (pig/boar) — appears as part of 象's original full-body pictograph of an elephant, reusing a four-legged-animal shape; 象 itself depicts an elephant's trunk and ears above the body.

example.hanzi: 他给我留下了很好的印象。
example.pinyin: Tā gěi wǒ liúxià le hěn hǎo de yìnxiàng.
example.english: He left a very good impression on me.
example.fact: 印象 combines 印 (“to stamp, print” — originally a hand pressing down a seal) with 象 (“image, shape,” from a pictograph of an elephant later broadened to mean any visual form) — together, “an image stamped [in the mind],” a metaphor strikingly close to English “impression,” from Latin “imprimere,” to press into.

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.hanzi: 她出生在一个小村庄。
example.pinyin: Tā chūshēng zài yí gè xiǎo cūnzhuāng.
example.english: She was born in a small village.
example.fact: 出生 is a resultative compound built from 出 (“to come out, exit”) and 生 (“to be born, to live”) — literally “to come out into life.” Grammatically it's a full verb, not an adjective, so English “born” (as in “I was born in 1990”) maps onto a verb phrase in Mandarin rather than a passive participle.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 进 relates to advancing or entering, both movement-related.
井 (jǐng) gives a close sound cue — 进 is pronounced jìn, sharing similar consonant and vowel sounds.
尸 (here representing a covering or stall, not a corpse) — 展 pictures a place where goods are displayed.
衣 (clothing) — clothing laid out for display gave 展 its meaning 'to unfold' or 'to exhibit.'

example.hanzi: 这项研究最近有了新的进展。
example.pinyin: Zhè xiàng yánjiū zuìjìn yǒule xīn de jìnzhǎn.
example.english: This research has recently made new progress.
example.fact: 进展 functions as both a noun (“progress,” as in 有进展, “there's progress”) and a verb (“to progress, make headway”) without changing form — one word doing double duty where English needs “progress” and “to progress” as two separate parts of speech.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 估 describes a person making a judgment or guess.
古 (gǔ) gives a sound close to gū, differing only in tone.
讠 (speech) — 计 relates to counting or planning through words and numbers.
十 (shí) gives a hint of the sound — 计 is pronounced jì, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 我估计这次旅行大概需要花费一万块钱。
example.pinyin: Wǒ gūjì zhè cì lǚxíng dàgài xūyào huāfèi yí wàn kuài qián.
example.english: I estimate this trip will cost around ten thousand yuan.
example.fact: In casual speech, 估计 has drifted from its literal sense “to calculate, estimate” into a hedging word much like English “I bet” or “I reckon” — saying 我估计他不会来了 (“I bet he's not coming”) doesn't require any actual arithmetic, just an informed hunch.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'
灬 (fire) — 点 originally related to a small flame or dot of light, giving rise to the meaning 'dot' or 'point.'
占 (zhàn) gives a hint of the sound — 点 is pronounced diǎn, a connection that has drifted over the centuries.

example.hanzi: 请把会议的时间和地点发给大家。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ huìyì de shíjiān hé dìdiǎn fā gěi dàjiā.
example.english: Please send everyone the time and location of the meeting.
example.fact: 地点 combines 地 (“ground, earth”) with 点 (“point, dot”) — literally “a point on the ground.” English arrives at a near-identical image from a different direction: “location” traces back to Latin “locus,” “place,” narrowed down to a specific spot.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.
王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 我需要跟经理谈一谈这个问题。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào gēn jīnglǐ tán yi tán zhège wèntí.
example.english: I need to have a talk with the manager about this problem.
example.fact: 经理 combines 经 (originally “the warp threads in weaving,” extended to “to manage, administer”) with 理 (originally “the natural grain in jade,” extended to “to put in order”) — two separate metaphors that had already drifted toward “to manage” before the compound was repurposed, under the influence of Western business terminology in the early 20th century, into the modern job title “manager” — a similar arc to how English “manager” itself grew out of the verb “to manage.”

components.note: 车 (cart) — 轻 originally described a light, nimble cart, extended to 'light (weight), gentle.'
工 (gōng) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from qīng.
木 (tree) — 松 names a type of tree, the pine.
公 (gōng) gives a rhyme close to sōng, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 考试终于结束了,大家都觉得很轻松。
example.pinyin: Kǎoshì zhōngyú jiéshù le, dàjiā dōu juéde hěn qīngsōng.
example.english: The exam is finally over, and everyone feels very relaxed.
example.fact: 轻松 pairs 轻 (“light, not heavy”) with 松 — but in this “loose, relaxed” sense, 松 is actually a simplification-era merger: traditional Chinese distinguishes 松 (“pine tree”) from 鬆 (“loose, slack, relaxed”), two originally separate characters that share only this single simplified form today.
